title: HE FELL INTO SIN. GOD FORGAVE HIM. BUT SHOULD HE EVER STAND BEHIND THE PULPIT AGAIN?
paragraphs: HE FELL INTO SIN. GOD FORGAVE HIM. BUT SHOULD HE EVER STAND BEHIND THE PULPIT AGAIN?

The question that could divide a church, expose a dangerous misunderstanding of grace, and force us to confront a truth many Christians would rather avoid: Jesus can restore a fallen pastor's soul without automatically restoring his authority.
Imagine walking into church on Sunday morning.
The worship team is singing. The congregation is standing. Hands are lifted. Some are crying. Others are whispering prayers only God can hear.
Then the pastor steps onto the platform.
The same pastor who once preached about holiness while secretly living in sin.
The same pastor who told struggling marriages to remain faithful while betraying his own vows.
The same pastor who stood before wounded people and proclaimed the healing power of Jesus Christ, only for those people to discover that he had been hiding something that shattered their trust.
And now he is back.
He holds a Bible.
His eyes fill with tears.
His voice trembles.
He says he has repented.
He says God has forgiven him.
He says the Lord has called him back into ministry.
And somewhere in that congregation sits a woman who still cannot sleep because of what happened.
Somewhere sits a husband whose faith was nearly destroyed.
Somewhere sits a young believer who once thought that pastor represented everything good about Christianity.
And somewhere sits another person who genuinely believes that refusing to welcome the pastor back into leadership means refusing to believe in the power of God's grace.
Two people can be sitting in the same church, listening to the same testimony, reading the same Bible, and carrying completely different kinds of pain.
One is afraid the church has forgotten mercy.
The other is afraid the church has forgotten justice.
And both deserve an answer rooted in Scripture rather than emotion, popularity, institutional survival, or personal loyalty.
So here is the question we cannot afford to answer carelessly.
If Jesus forgives a fallen pastor, does that mean the church must give him the pulpit back?
Before you answer, remember something.
The person asking may not be the pastor who fell.
It may be someone who was hurt when he fell.
And how we answer may determine whether that person ever feels safe walking into a church again.
The Gospel does not require us to choose between grace and truth.
Jesus Christ is full of both.
John 1:14 describes Him as "full of grace and truth."
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And if we separate what Jesus perfectly holds together, we can end up calling cruelty holiness or calling compromise compassion.
We need to understand what Scripture actually teaches.
Because a pastor's repentance matters deeply.
But so do the people his sin affected.
And so does the holiness of Christ's Church.
There is a difference between being forgiven by God and being qualified to lead God's people.
That distinction may be one of the most important truths the modern Church needs to recover.
Consider the apostle Paul's words in 1 Timothy 3:2.
The Greek text begins:
δεῖ οὖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι
Dei oun ton episkopon anepilēmpton einai.
A faithful translation is:
"Therefore an overseer must be above reproach."
Notice that word.
ἀνεπίλημπτον — anepilēmpton.
It describes someone who is not legitimately open to reproach in the relevant sense, someone whose character can withstand serious scrutiny.
It does not mean sinless perfection.
If it did, no human pastor could ever qualify.
But it does mean that spiritual leadership requires a demonstrable pattern of integrity.
Paul does not say that an overseer must be gifted enough to attract a crowd.
He does not say he must be charismatic enough to move people emotionally.
He does not say his sermons must generate thousands of views.
He says he must be above reproach.
Then Paul speaks of marital faithfulness, self-control, respectable conduct, hospitality, the ability to teach, gentleness, freedom from greed, and responsible care for one's household.
In Titus 1:7, he writes:
δεῖ γὰρ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνέγκλητον εἶναι
Dei gar ton episkopon anenklēton einai.
"For an overseer must be blameless."
The Greek word anegklēton carries the sense of being free from a sustainable accusation of wrongdoing.
Again, this is not a demand for moral perfection.
It is a demand for credible moral fitness.
And that changes the conversation.
Because when a pastor commits serious sin, the question is not merely whether God can forgive him.
Of course God can.
The question is whether that pastor currently possesses the biblical qualifications necessary to shepherd souls.
And forgiveness alone does not settle that question.
A man may be genuinely repentant and still be unqualified for pastoral leadership.
A man may be deeply loved by God and still need to step away permanently from the office he once held.
A man may be restored to fellowship without being restored to authority.
And none of those realities diminish the blood of Jesus Christ.
They honor the seriousness of the responsibility entrusted to a shepherd.
Think about King David.
David was not an unbeliever who accidentally wandered into the story of redemption.
He was a man chosen by God.
A worshiper.
A poet.
A warrior.
A king whose psalms would comfort generations of broken believers.
Yet David committed adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrated the death of her husband, Uriah.
Read 2 Samuel 11 carefully.
This was not merely a private moral failure.
It involved the misuse of royal power, the destruction of another man's life, and devastating harm inflicted upon others.
Then Nathan confronted him.
David confessed:
"I have sinned against the LORD." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
And Nathan answered:
"The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die."
What extraordinary mercy.
David was forgiven.
But read what happened next.
His sin still brought grievous consequences.
His family endured terrible suffering.
The sword did not depart from his house.
His confession was real, but it did not erase the damage.
And we must be careful here.
David's continuation as king was part of a particular Old Testament royal history. It is not a New Testament command to reinstate pastors after serious misconduct.
We cannot take a descriptive account of Israel's monarchy and use it to override the qualifications Christ's apostles established for Church leadership.
David's story proves that God's mercy can reach a grievous sinner.
It does not prove that every forgiven leader must regain the position he abused.
Now consider Peter.
Perhaps you are already thinking about him.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Not once.
Three times.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met him beside the Sea of Galilee.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter whether he loved Him.
Then came the words:
"Feed my sheep." (John 21:17, KJV)
It was a breathtaking moment of restoration.
A man who had denied knowing Jesus was commissioned to care for those who belonged to Jesus.
Surely, someone might argue, that settles everything.
If Peter was restored, why should a fallen pastor not be restored?
But Scripture requires us to examine more than the emotional similarity.

Peter's denial was serious and shameful. Yet the account does not describe him exploiting vulnerable congregants, committing sexual abuse, manipulating people under pastoral authority, or concealing a prolonged pattern of predatory behavior.
His restoration was also personally and authoritatively given by the risen Christ.
And Jesus' command was not an unrestricted permission slip for every fallen leader in every circumstance.
In fact, the language Jesus used should make every pastor tremble.
βόσκε τὰ πρόβατά μου
Boske ta probata mou.
"Feed my sheep."
My sheep.
Not your sheep.
Not your platform.
Not your audience.
Not your ministry empire.
My sheep.
Jesus was reminding Peter that the flock belonged to Christ.
And that means no pastor has an inherent right to reclaim leadership over people he has harmed.
The sheep are not trophies awarded to a leader for completing a repentance process.
They belong to the Shepherd who purchased them with His own blood.
Acts 20:28 reminds church overseers that the flock is God's Church, obtained through His blood.
That truth should change the way every congregation handles pastoral failure.
Because when a leader falls, the first question must never be, "How quickly can we rebuild his ministry?"
It must be, "How do we honor Christ, protect His people, establish the truth, and respond faithfully to everyone affected?"
Sometimes the most Christlike decision a church can make is to refuse to put a fallen pastor back into leadership.
Even when he cries.
Even when he apologizes.
Even when he has supporters.
Even when his preaching is powerful.
Even when the congregation misses him.
And even when his repentance appears sincere.
That may sound harsh until we remember who pastoral leadership is supposed to serve.
The shepherd exists for the sheep.
The sheep do not exist to rehabilitate the shepherd's reputation.
There is a warning in Ezekiel 34 that should haunt anyone entrusted with spiritual authority.
God rebuked the shepherds of Israel because they fed themselves while neglecting the flock.
In Ezekiel 34:4, the Lord condemned them for failing to strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the straying, and seek the lost.
Instead, they ruled with force and harshness.
Then God declared that He Himself would seek His sheep.
Do you hear the heart of the Father?
He did not dismiss the suffering of the flock to preserve the dignity of the shepherds.
He confronted the shepherds because the flock mattered.
And that is precisely why the Church must take spiritual abuse, sexual misconduct, financial exploitation, intimidation, manipulation, and serious dishonesty with extraordinary seriousness.
When a pastor uses spiritual authority to exploit someone, the harm can extend far beyond the immediate act.
It can distort a person's understanding of God.
A victim may struggle to pray because the voice that once taught them to pray belonged to the person who betrayed them.
A young believer may begin associating Scripture with manipulation.
A family may stop attending church, not because they stopped loving Jesus, but because the place where they expected safety became the place where they were wounded.
And when that happens, telling wounded people to "just forgive and move on" can become another act of spiritual harm.
Forgiveness is biblical.
Coerced silence is not.
Reconciliation is precious.
Forced access is not.
Grace is glorious.
But grace does not require the vulnerable to surrender their safety.
A person can forgive a pastor and still testify truthfully about what happened.
A person can forgive and still report criminal conduct to the proper authorities.
A person can forgive and still refuse contact.
A person can forgive and still believe that the former pastor should never again exercise spiritual authority.
And a church can affirm that forgiveness while pursuing accountability.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of civil authority in restraining and responding to wrongdoing.

Criminal abuse should be reported to the appropriate authorities, and churches should comply with applicable reporting laws, preserve evidence, and never substitute internal counseling for lawful investigation.
Allegations must be assessed fairly, without presuming guilt or dismissing complainants.
Protecting people and honoring due process are not opposing commitments.
They are both necessary.
Now listen carefully, because this is where the discussion becomes deeply personal.
What if the pastor truly repents?
What if there is no performance?
No excuses.
No blaming the devil, the congregation, the spouse, the victim, the pressure of ministry, or some mysterious spiritual attack.
What if he looks at the wreckage and finally says:
"I did this. I sinned against God. I harmed people. I have no right to demand my position back."
What then?
Then we should rejoice that repentance may be taking root.
Not because consequences have disappeared.
But because a sinner is turning toward the mercy of Christ.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is:
μετάνοια — metanoia.
It refers to a change of mind or heart that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling embarrassed because the truth became public.
It is not crying because donations stopped.
It is not apologizing because a ministry brand collapsed.
It is not saying, "I made mistakes," when those "mistakes" were deliberate acts that harmed real people.
Biblical repentance faces the truth.
And true repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist declared:
"Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance." (Matthew 3:8, KJV)
In Greek, the phrase includes:
καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας
Karpon axion tēs metanoias.
"Fruit worthy of repentance."
Fruit.
Not just words.
Not just tears.
Not just an emotional testimony set to beautiful background music.
Fruit.

That fruit may include full and truthful confession, cooperation with independent investigations, accepting lawful consequences, making restitution where possible, relinquishing authority, pursuing appropriate professional care, and demonstrating changed conduct over a substantial period of time.
And here is a difficult truth.
A pastor who is genuinely repentant should be willing to accept the possibility that obedience to Jesus means never becoming a pastor again.
Because repentance is not a negotiation in which we surrender our sin in exchange for getting our old position back.
Repentance is surrendering ourselves to God.
Even when His will leads somewhere we did not want to go.
Even when our reputation cannot be recovered.
Even when the consequences last longer than the tears.
Even when the only ministry left to us is living quietly, working honestly, caring for our family, and worshiping Jesus without a microphone.
Can a man still love Christ when nobody applauds him?
Can he still serve God when his name is no longer on the church sign?
Can he still rejoice when another faithful pastor takes the position he once held?
Can he still say, "Jesus is enough," when Jesus does not give him his platform back?
Those questions may reveal more about repentance than a hundred public apologies.
Because the goal of salvation is not the restoration of our celebrity.
The goal is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more beautiful than our religious instincts sometimes allow.
Jesus did not die merely to make bad leaders respectable again.
He died to save sinners.
Every kind of sinner.
The proud pastor.
The wounded church member who has become consumed by bitterness.
The person hiding pornography behind a respectable Christian image.
The woman drowning in shame over a secret she has never confessed.
The man who keeps promising God that this will be the last time.
The believer who is exhausted from pretending to be stronger than he really is.
The religious person who knows all the right verses but has forgotten how desperately he needs mercy.
All of us stand before the same holy God.
And none of us can purchase forgiveness with religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις — charis.
Grace is God's undeserved favor.
It is not a reward for people who have successfully repaired their public image.
It is not a certificate of moral achievement.
It is God's gracious gift to people who cannot save themselves.
And the cross is where that grace is displayed with staggering clarity.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, suffered for sinners.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The risen Christ offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
But notice something about that grace.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon sin.
Grace teaches us to turn away from it.
Grace does not make accountability unnecessary.
Grace changes our relationship with truth.
Grace does not turn a pulpit into an entitlement.
Grace teaches us that Christ is worthy of obedience whether or not anyone ever hands us a microphone again.
This is why the distinction between restoration to fellowship and restoration to leadership matters so much.
Galatians 6:1 calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in transgression with gentleness, while remaining watchful over themselves.
The Greek verb translated "restore" is related to:
καταρτίζω — katartizō.
It can mean to mend, put in order, or restore to a proper condition.
But Galatians 6:1 does not say that every restored believer must return to a former position of authority.
It calls for spiritual restoration.
That is not identical to reinstatement in pastoral office.
A fallen pastor who repents should not automatically be treated as beyond the reach of Christian love.
He may need pastoral care, discipleship, accountability, counseling, and the patient fellowship of mature believers.
He may need help learning to live as a faithful Christian without being the person in charge.
And depending on the nature of the offense, he may need strict boundaries, legal accountability, and permanent exclusion from positions involving vulnerable people.
That is not necessarily abandonment.
Sometimes that is what responsible care looks like.
But what about returning to leadership?
Is it ever possible?
We must be careful not to claim more than Scripture explicitly states.
The New Testament does not give one universal timetable or a single restoration procedure covering every kind of pastoral sin.
It does, however, establish qualifications for elders and overseers, command impartial accountability, and warn against hasty appointments.
In 1 Timothy 5:19–20, Paul gives instructions concerning accusations against elders, requiring adequate witnesses and addressing elders who persist in sin.
In verse 21, he commands impartiality.
And in verse 22, he warns against laying hands on anyone hastily.
These instructions do not allow a church to ignore serious accusations because a pastor is influential.
Nor do they permit condemnation without fair examination.
A church must pursue truth.

In cases involving serious wrongdoing, credible independent investigation and safeguarding measures may be essential, particularly when the pastor's own leadership structure has conflicts of interest.
And the nature of the offense matters.

A pastor who experiences a serious moral failure, voluntarily confesses, submits to correction, and demonstrates lasting repentance presents a different situation from a pastor who repeatedly exploits people, threatens witnesses, conceals abuse, or uses spiritual authority to manipulate victims.
Those distinctions are morally significant.
Some churches, after lengthy and independent evaluation, may conclude that a formerly disqualified leader has again become biblically qualified for a particular ministry role.
Other churches, equally committed to Scripture, may conclude that certain serious violations of pastoral trust permanently disqualify someone from the pastoral office.
Faithful Christians disagree about whether particular offenses can ever be followed by requalification.
But they should not disagree about the need to protect the flock, establish the facts, uphold biblical standards, and refuse to treat public remorse as sufficient proof of fitness.
There is no biblical rule that says six months of counseling automatically restores a pastor.
There is no biblical guarantee that a year away from preaching makes a person trustworthy.
There is no spiritual formula in which enough tears, enough testimonies, and enough supportive church members erase the requirements of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1.
And no congregation should ever be pressured to accept a leader's return simply because he claims God told him to resume preaching.
A claimed calling must be tested by Scripture.
Spiritual authority is not self-certified.
A leader who truly fears God should welcome appropriate scrutiny rather than demand immunity from it.
James 3:1 says:
"My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation." (KJV)
The word translated "masters" in the King James Version refers here to teachers.
James warns that those who teach will face stricter judgment.
That is sobering.
Because the pulpit is not simply a place where a talented communicator performs.
It is a place where people are taught to trust God's Word.
And when a pastor's conduct seriously contradicts that Word, the damage can be profound.
Sometimes churches make the mistake of treating a gifted pastor as irreplaceable.
"He built this ministry."
"Thousands came to Christ under his preaching."
"Nobody can preach like him."
"Look how much God used him."
But spiritual gifting is not proof of present spiritual qualification.
And past fruit does not cancel present accountability.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that extraordinary religious activity is not, by itself, proof of a right relationship with Him.
That warning should make us deeply cautious about confusing visible ministry success with holiness.
A crowded sanctuary is not a moral defense.
A large following is not evidence that an accusation is false.
A powerful sermon cannot undo an act of exploitation.
And a church that sacrifices truth to preserve a ministry's public image may end up protecting the institution while abandoning the people it was called to serve.
Jesus does not need us to hide sin to protect His reputation.
His truth is not that fragile.
His Church does not become stronger through secrecy.
And His Gospel is not honored when victims are treated as obstacles to a leader's comeback story.
Perhaps the most painful part of this entire conversation is that some of the people who have been hurt by fallen pastors still love those pastors.
They remember the good moments.
The hospital visits.
The prayers during family crises.
The sermons that helped them survive depression.
The baptism.
The wedding.
The funeral where the pastor spoke words that brought genuine comfort.
And now they are trying to reconcile those memories with the terrible things they have learned.
They do not know whether to grieve, rage, forgive, leave, stay, or question everything.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to pretend the good memories never happened.
And you do not have to deny the harm because some good memories remain.
Both can be true.
God may have used a sermon to comfort you even if the person preaching it was living dishonestly.
The truth of Scripture does not become false because the messenger was unfaithful.
But neither does the truth of Scripture excuse the messenger's unfaithfulness.
Your faith was never supposed to rest on a pastor's perfection.
It was meant to rest on Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 13:8 declares:
"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." (KJV)
The pastor changed.
The institution may have failed.
People you trusted may have disappointed you.
But Jesus has not ceased to be holy.
He has not ceased to be merciful.
He has not ceased to care for the wounded.
And He has not abandoned His sheep.
If your experience has left you unable to trust church leadership, you are not required to rush your healing to make other people comfortable.
Seek safe, trustworthy support.
Take time to discern.
Ask difficult questions.
Remember that Jesus never commanded you to confuse blind loyalty to a religious leader with loyalty to Himself.
And if you are a pastor reading this, perhaps this is the moment to examine your own heart.
Not the pastor whose scandal is circulating online.
Yours.
What are you hiding?
What have you justified because you were tired, lonely, powerful, admired, or convinced that your ministry was too important to fail?
Are you becoming more accountable as your influence grows?
Or are you becoming harder to correct?
Do you have people who can confront you without fear?
Or have you surrounded yourself with people whose livelihoods depend on agreeing with you?
Do you love the sheep?
Or do you love being needed by them?
There is still time to tell the truth before a hidden sin becomes another family's tragedy.
There is still time to step into the light.
There is still time to seek help, relinquish control, and turn to Christ.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to conceal wrongdoing.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
And perhaps the most radical act of obedience a compromised leader can perform is to tell the truth without first calculating what it will cost him.
Not every story of grace ends with the man returning to the pulpit.
Some stories end with a former pastor sitting quietly in the back row, worshiping the Savior he once publicly represented.
Some end with a man working an ordinary job, paying restitution, accepting accountability, and learning that his identity was never supposed to be his title.
Some end with a family slowly rebuilding trust.
Some end with wounded people finding safety in a different congregation.
Some end with justice being pursued and survivors finally being heard.
Some involve reconciliation.
Others do not.
But where genuine repentance and faith in Christ are present, grace is not absent simply because a former position is never restored.
Because the greatest restoration Jesus offers is not a return to status.
It is reconciliation with God.
And that brings us to the scandal at the center of the Gospel itself.
Not a scandal of hidden corruption.
But the astonishing grace of a holy Savior who willingly died for the ungodly.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Before we cleaned up our reputations.
Before we learned the right religious language.
Before we could offer anything that would make us worthy.
Christ died for us.
That is the Gospel.
But the same Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners also commands His people to walk in the light.
He is the Savior of the guilty and the Defender of the vulnerable.
He is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
And He will never ask His Church to sacrifice those sheep on the altar of a pastor's reputation.
So should a pastor who falls into serious sin ever return to ministry leadership?
The biblical answer is neither an automatic yes nor a careless universal no for every circumstance.

Forgiveness is available through Christ. Restoration to Christian fellowship should be pursued appropriately where genuine repentance is present. But return to pastoral leadership is a separate matter, governed by biblical qualifications, the nature and consequences of the offense, demonstrable character, impartial evaluation, and the safety of the flock.
In some cases, a carefully evaluated return may be possible.
In other cases, permanent removal from pastoral authority is the faithful and necessary outcome.
And when serious abuse or exploitation is involved, the protection of others must never be compromised to engineer a comeback.
The Church must not confuse mercy with reinstatement.
Nor must it confuse accountability with a denial of redemption.
We can love a fallen pastor without giving him a congregation to lead.
We can pray for his salvation without defending his misconduct.
We can believe Jesus has forgiven him without demanding that wounded people trust him again.
We can celebrate repentance without celebrating the restoration of power.
And we can insist on truth without surrendering compassion.
That is not a weak Gospel.
That is a Gospel strong enough to face reality.
And maybe, beneath all our arguments about fallen pastors, there is another question waiting for us.
What do we actually believe makes a person valuable?
Their position?
Their popularity?
Their gifts?
Their influence?
Or the fact that Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never earn His mercy?
If a man loses his pulpit but gains a life of humble obedience to Christ, he has not lost everything.
If a wounded believer loses trust in a human shepherd but discovers the faithfulness of the Good Shepherd, that believer has not been abandoned.
And if a church loses a famous leader but chooses holiness, accountability, and care for the vulnerable, it may discover that its greatest testimony was never the man behind the microphone.
It was the Lord Jesus Christ.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus erases consequences.
Not that every scandal deserves a comeback tour.
Not that repentance is proven by returning to public ministry.
But that the grace of Christ can bring truth into darkness, repentance into hardened hearts, healing into wounded lives, and hope into circumstances that once seemed beyond redemption.
Jesus rewrites everything because He is not merely interested in restoring appearances.
He transforms hearts.
And He calls His people to follow Him in truth.
If this article has confronted something you have been carrying, I want to hear from you.
Maybe you are a pastor who needs the courage to stop hiding.
Maybe you are a believer who has been deeply wounded by church leadership.
Maybe you have been struggling to understand how forgiveness and accountability can exist together.
Or perhaps you have watched someone you love fall into sin, and you are still trying to understand what grace should look like afterward.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose someone else's story publicly. You can ask for prayer without explaining everything.
And if God has brought you through a season of repentance, healing, or restoration, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Be honest.
Have we sometimes become so determined to restore fallen leaders that we have forgotten to care for the people they hurt?
And how can churches demonstrate both biblical mercy and genuine accountability?
I would value your thoughtful response.
Not because every comment will agree.
But because this conversation matters.
And somewhere, someone may read your words and realize they are not alone.

If this message has helped you understand Scripture more clearly, please save it. There may come a day when you need to revisit the difference between forgiveness and qualification, between repentance and reinstatement, between grace and the misuse of grace.
Not to stir up hostility or turn someone's suffering into entertainment, but to help other believers think carefully and biblically about a question that affects real lives.
One thoughtful share may reach a church member who has been pressured into silence.
It may reach a pastor who needs to repent before more damage is done.
It may reach a struggling believer who desperately needs to know that Jesus is not the same as the leader who betrayed their trust.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown spiritually weary, the person who has walked away from church, and even the seeker who is not yet sure what to believe.
Here we want to keep returning to the truth of God's Word, the necessity of repentance, the beauty of grace, the reality of forgiveness, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
But I also want to extend a more personal invitation.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical teaching, Christian encouragement, discipleship resources, and the message of salvation through Jesus Christ.
People who are grieving.
People who are hiding.
People who are searching.
People who have almost given up.
And people who need to hear that the grace of Christ is still greater than the darkness they are facing.

Scripture encourages believers to support faithful Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
God does not measure your love for Him by whether you can afford a monthly payment.

These resources and products are not what makes discipleship possible. Jesus and His Word remain central. But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth and help sustain the work we are seeking to do.
Those free resources matter because biblical encouragement should never be limited only to those who can afford to pay.
But the Gospel is not for sale.
Because at the end of everything, this ministry is not supposed to be about building a personality.
It is about pointing people to the Person of Jesus Christ.
The One who never abused His authority.
The One who never betrayed His sheep.
The One who never concealed sin, because He had no sin to conceal.
The One who could have demanded service from everyone, yet humbled Himself and washed His disciples' feet.
The One who went to the cross, not to protect His reputation, but to redeem sinners.
The One who rose again and remains the true Shepherd of His people.

And one day, when every pulpit is silent, every platform has disappeared, every title has lost its importance, and every human leader stands before God, only one name will remain worthy of our worship.
Jesus Christ.
So let the fallen repent.
Let the wounded be heard.
Let the truth be established.
Let justice be pursued.
Let the Church be protected.
Let forgiveness be proclaimed.
And let every decision about leadership bow before the authority of God's Word.
Because the most important question is not whether a fallen pastor can stand behind a pulpit again.
It is whether all of us are willing to bow before Jesus Christ, even when obedience costs us everything we once thought defined us.
A pulpit can be lost forever, and a soul can still be saved forever—because Jesus came to redeem sinners, not to preserve their thrones.
